skill.name: Bare claim or backed-up claim
skill.why: Anyone can say anything. A backed-up claim gives you something to check.
skill.how: Find the claim. Then look for a reason or proof holding it up.

beats.say: A claim is something a writer wants you to believe.
beats.show: **Mo's pies are the best on Bluster Rock.**

beats.say: A bare claim stands alone. Nothing holds it up.
beats.show: Mo's pies are the best. **Buy one now!**

beats.say: A backed-up claim comes with a reason or some proof.
beats.show: Mo's pies are the best. **They won first prize at the show.**

beats.say: Saying it again, or louder, is not backing.
beats.show: Mo's pies are the best! **THE BEST!**

beats.say: Backing must fit the claim. A random fact holds nothing up.
beats.show: Mo's pies are the best. **Pies are round.**

weDo.hint: Which one gives you something you could check?
weDo.success: The four-metre test holds the claim up. The others just say it again, or tell you to buy.

options.reason: 'Seriously, it is!' just says the claim again. Nothing holds it up.

encounters.text: This week, the Bugle asked readers about the Bluster Rock Primary school band. Should it get more money from the council? Here are some of the claims readers sent in. encounters.frame: Coach Dev Marsh is writing to the Bluster Rock Bugle. The Bilbolster is checking his draft for backing.
encounters.text: Dear Editor, I coach the Bluster Rock Roos, our town's junior footy team. Our home ground is the oval at Red Dune Park, and I am writing to ask the council to put lights on it. Every winter, the sun sets before 5:30 pm, and by the time the kids finish school and get to the oval, there is barely an hour of daylight left. The oval needs lights. I have coached here for eleven years, and I have watched this problem get worse every season. Parents have offered to run a sausage sizzle at every home game to help raise money. Our players are aged from eight to twelve, and we have three teams. I have one more sentence to add to this letter, and I want it to give readers a real reason to agree with me. I would be grateful if the council could discuss this at its next meeting. Yours sincerely, Dev Marsh, coach of the Bluster Rock Roos

encounters.frame: The Year 6 debate on canteen food got heated. The Bilbolster took notes with its ears.
encounters.text: On Thursday, Year 6 held a debate in the library about what the Bluster Rock Primary canteen should sell. One team argued for healthier food, and the other argued for keeping the menu just as it is. Mo was the timekeeper, although he kept stopping the clock to tell jokes about sausages. The healthy-food team wore green T-shirts, and the keep-the-menu team brought a giant cardboard pie as a mascot. At one point, the pie fell over and knocked a jug of water onto the judges' notes. Year 5 students in the audience were asked to listen carefully and write down every claim they heard. Both teams made lots of claims. Some were backed up with real reasons or proof. Others sounded convincing but had nothing holding them up. Watch out for reasons that just say the claim again in different words, and for 'proof' that has nothing to do with the claim. Principal Okafor will read the best arguments at assembly next week.
encounters.prompt: Put each claim from the debate in the right box. A backed-up claim has a reason that actually supports it.
encounters.success: Backing has to show why the claim is true. Repeating it, or adding an unrelated fact, holds nothing up.

encounters.frame: Ada Pennick is drafting a second letter about the turtles. The Bilbolster is reading it from a rock pool.
encounters.text: Dear Editor, Last month, I wrote to object to jet ski hire in Bluster Bay, and many readers have asked me why I am so certain that jet skis are hurting the turtles. It is a fair question. The northern end of the bay has been a nesting beach for green turtles for as long as anyone can remember, and every summer, volunteers like me count the nests, fence them off and watch the hatchlings scramble down to the water. Until this year, injured turtles were rare. Each nest holds around a hundred eggs, and the hatchlings come out at night, guided by the moonlight on the water. Jet skis are allowed in the bay from 7 am to 7 pm, seven days a week, and the hire shop has twelve of them. On a busy Saturday, all twelve are out on the water at once. I am not against fun, and I am not against tourists, who bring welcome money to our town. But I believe that jet skis are hurting the turtles, and I want to show readers why. I have one sentence left to write before I send this letter, and I want it to be the strongest backing I can give. The council will vote on the jet ski hire licence on 12 December. Yours faithfully, Ada Pennick, turtle volunteer
encounters.prompt: Ada claims jet skis are hurting the turtles. Which sentence would back up her claim best?
encounters.success: Propeller-shaped cuts appearing since the hire shop opened is real proof. It links the injuries to jet skis.

options.text: Jet skis are clearly a menace, as anyone with eyes can see.
options.reason: 'As anyone can see' asks you to agree without showing anything. The claim stays bare.

options.text: Green turtles have been swimming in the world's oceans for more than 100 million years.
options.reason: This is an impressive fact, but it says nothing about whether jet skis hurt them.

options.text: The company that runs the hire shop also sponsors Maxx Vantablack's channel.
options.reason: This might make you distrust the company, but it isn't proof that jet skis hurt turtles.

options.text: Since the hire shop opened, rangers have found fourteen turtles with propeller cuts.

encounters.frame: Maxx is defending his art auction in the comments. The Bilbolster is trying very hard to find any backing.
encounters.text: Maxx it out, Vantafam! So, some of you have been leaving comments about my painting, 'Gold on Gold', which sold last night for $40,000. A few haters are saying it was just a canvas with gold paint splashed on it, and one person, who I won't name, said it looked like a dropped pancake. Let me tell you a bit about the painting first. It's two metres wide, it's covered in real gold leaf, and I finished it in a single afternoon, between my morning workout and my afternoon hair appointment. The frame alone weighs twelve kilograms. The buyer is a mystery collector from overseas, who has asked me not to say their name, but I can tell you they have excellent taste. They also bought my sunglasses. Well, I've decided to answer every complaint, one by one, because that's the kind of transparent, honest streamer I am. I've also included a few comments from my biggest supporters, who wrote in to defend me, and some of them make excellent points. Read them all, and then decide for yourself who's right. Spoiler: it's me. Remember, every cent from the auction goes to the Maxx Vantablack Rescue Fund, so if you complain, you're basically complaining about rescued Creatures. That's Maxx-imum content! Stay gold!
encounters.prompt: Put each comment in the right box.
encounters.success: Backing must show why the claim is true. Insults, repetition and unrelated facts hold nothing up.

bins: backed-up claim: a reason or proof that supports it

items.text: The painting is valuable, because a collector paid $40,000 for it at a public auction.
items.reason: A real sale price is proof of what someone thought it was worth.

items.text: The painting is a work of genius, because only a genius could have painted it.
items.reason: The reason only says 'genius' again. The claim holds itself up, so it's bare.

items.text: Anyone who doesn't like the painting is just jealous of Maxx.
items.reason: Calling critics jealous is an attack, not a reason. Nothing supports the claim.

items.text: The painting took real skill, because Maxx spent three years at art school learning to use gold leaf.
items.reason: Three years of training is a reason to think skill was needed.

items.text: The painting is beautiful, because the auction was held in a fancy hotel with 300 rooms.
items.reason: A hotel's size says nothing about the painting itself. It doesn't support the claim.

items.text: The money reached the Rescue Fund, because the fund's bank records show $40,000 arriving this morning.
items.reason: Bank records are proof you could check. They support the claim that the money arrived.

encounters.frame: A local band has written to the Bluster Rock Bugle. The Bilbolster is tapping its foot and its ears.
encounters.prompt: The band claims a festival would be good for local shops. Tap the sentence that backs up this claim.
encounters.success: Takings doubling last time is proof a festival brings shoppers. That backs up the claim directly.

parts: Dear Editor, We are Red Dust Static, a band that started in a garage behind the Bluster Rock service station four years ago. We are writing to ask the council to bring back the Bluster Rock Music Festival, which has not been held since 2019. We believe a festival would be good for local shops.

parts.tap: Without any doubt whatsoever, a festival is exactly what this town's shops need most.
parts.reason: Being very certain isn't the same as giving proof. This just says the claim more strongly.

parts.tap: Music has been bringing people together for thousands of years, in every culture on Earth.
parts.reason: This may be true, but it's about music in general. It doesn't show shops would benefit.

parts.tap: At the last festival, the bakery, the service station and the newsagent all reported that their takings doubled for the weekend.
Our drummer's grandmother, who has lived here for seventy years, played the piano at the very first festival.
parts.reason: This is a nice piece of history, but it says nothing about local shops.

parts: We would happily play for free, and three other local bands have already offered to join us. We have even found a stage: the old flatbed truck behind the footy club, which only needs new tyres and a very thorough clean. If the council agrees, we could hold the festival next autumn, when the evenings are cool and the flies have mostly given up. Yours sincerely, Jojo, Sunny and Dax, Red Dust Static

encounters.frame: Gus is preparing a speech for the school council. The Bilbolster has spotted a reason that isn't one.
encounters.text: Gus has always loved taking things apart, and he once rebuilt a toaster so that it could launch toast across the kitchen. For three years, Gus has been asking Bluster Rock Primary to start a robotics club. This term, the school council has finally agreed to listen, and Gus has five minutes to make his case at Thursday's meeting. He has spent the week preparing. He has borrowed a robot kit from the Bluster Rock library and built a small robot that can sort recycling into the right bins. He tested it on the contents of the staffroom rubbish bin, which he describes as 'a scientific experience'. The robot is called Sorty, and it has a camera eye, two claws made from salad tongs and a conveyor belt that used to be part of a treadmill. During the staffroom test, Sorty sorted forty-one out of fifty items correctly. It did, however, put a teabag in the paper bin and a banana skin on Principal Okafor's chair. He has also collected the names of students who want to join. His speech ends with three reasons, but Wren has pointed out that one of them doesn't actually give the council a reason to agree. Gus would like to fix it before Thursday, preferably without starting again.
encounters.prompt: Tap the reason that doesn't back up Gus's claim. Then choose a real one.
encounters.success: Twenty-six students signing up is proof the club would be used. The weak reason just said 'robotics clubs are good'.

parts: The school should start a robotics club, because

parts.tap: the library will lend us robot kits for free
parts.reason: That's real backing. Free kits show the club could start without big costs.

parts: , because

parts.tap: my sorting robot shows that students can build useful machines
parts.reason: That's real backing. The robot is proof of what students could do.

parts: , and because

parts.tap: a robotics club is a good thing for a school to have

options.text: robots are the future, and the future is robots
options.reason: This sounds clever, but it says the same thing twice. It doesn't back up the claim.

options.text: twenty-six students have already signed up to join
nobody with any sense could possibly say no
options.reason: This pressures the council but gives no reason. The claim stays bare.

options.text: I have personally wanted one for three whole years
options.reason: Wanting something for a long time isn't a reason the school should do it.

encounters.frame: Four companies want to sell their products at the Vantamart. The Bilbolster is reading their pitches with its nose held.
encounters.text: Every month, the Vantamart's buyers listen to pitches from companies that want their products on its shelves. This month's theme is 'Gross but Good', and four companies have been shortlisted. The first sells a toothpaste made from crushed seashells. The second sells a spray that makes old socks smell like fresh lemons. The third sells a slime that glows in the dark, and the fourth sells a soap that is shaped like a cane toad. Each company was allowed to send one short claim to the buyers, along with whatever backing it chose to include. Maxx will make the final decision himself, after he has tried every product live on his stream. The buyers have asked for claims that are short and clear, because they read hundreds of them every month. Last month's winner was a burping water bottle that sold out in three days. Whichever product wins will be sold in every Vantamart and advertised on Maxx's stream for a whole month. The products will be judged on how well they sell, how gross they are and, in Maxx's words, 'how good they look next to my face'. Gus has asked for free samples of all four, and Mo has asked whether any of them are edible.
encounters.prompt: Which company's pitch is a bare claim?
encounters.success: The day the soap was invented says nothing about how good it is. The soap pitch has no real backing.

options.text: Our toothpaste cleans well, because a dentist tested it on 200 people and found less plaque after a month.
options.reason: A dentist's test on 200 people is proof you could check. This claim is backed up.

options.text: Our spray removes sock smells, because it contains a chemical that breaks down the germs that cause the stink.
options.reason: Breaking down the germs that cause the smell is a reason it works. This claim is backed up.

options.text: Our slime is safe for children, because it passed every test set by the national toy safety board.
options.reason: Passing safety tests is proof. This claim is backed up.

options.text: Our toad-shaped soap is the best soap ever made, because it was invented on a Tuesday in 2019.

encounters.frame: Slick Vinnie has written a notice about the mystery lights. The Bilbolster is reading it by torchlight.
encounters.prompt: Vinnie makes four claims in a row. Tap the one with nothing backing it up.
encounters.success: A $10 ticket doesn't show the tour is the only way to see the lights. The other claims have backing.

parts: A NOTICE FROM SLICK VINNIE, TOUR GUIDE. As you will have read in the Bugle, strange green lights have been appearing above the old mine at the back of Bluster Rock. People have been asking me about them all week, so here is what I can tell you.

parts.tap: The lights are real, because a security camera at the service station filmed them on Tuesday night.
parts.reason: Security camera footage is proof you could check. This claim is backed up.

parts.tap: The lights appear at the same time each night, because they have been seen at about 11:40 pm three nights in a row.
parts.reason: Three sightings at the same time are proof of a pattern. This claim is backed up.

parts.tap: The mine is unsafe to enter alone, because the council's engineers found two collapsed tunnels in last year's inspection.
parts.reason: An engineers' inspection is proof the tunnels are dangerous. This claim is backed up.

parts.tap: My midnight tour is the only way to see the lights properly, because tickets are just $10.

parts: Tickets are now $10, up from $5, due to what I'm calling 'ghost demand'. Bring a torch, a warm jumper and a sense of adventure. The Soggy Biscuit crew has asked whether I have anything to do with the lights. I would like to say, very clearly, that I do not, and that the box of green glow sticks in my ute belongs to my cousin.
